passage:
On Monday, Bhupen presented the new tracker layout to the team as if he had drawn it up himself. Avni had sketched it in a chat on Thursday. Her face went hot and her jaw tightened, and she felt used. She nearly stood up and said so in front of everyone. Instead she stayed silent through the meeting.

That afternoon she collected the chat messages and the dated drafts. She asked Bhupen for five minutes. "That layout came from my Thursday message. Next time, can we say whose idea it was?" Bhupen shifted. "I built on it." "You did, and I want it to be clear." She began sending her updates in writing to the whole team, and at the start of any project she said what each person owned. If it happened again, she decided, she would take the dated messages to the manager as plain facts.

Amandeep, seated beside her, seethed in another way. When Bhupen's promotion was announced a month later, Amandeep felt bitter and had nothing kind to say in the pantry. Then Avni said, "Show your work. Post your fixes in the weekly notes." Amandeep began writing a Friday summary of what had been done and by whom. By the next review, the manager was quoting it.

qa.q: When had Avni sketched the tracker layout?
qa.a: She had sketched it in a chat on Thursday.

qa.q: How did Avni's handling of the credit-taking differ from Amandeep's reaction to Bhupen's promotion?
qa.a: Avni collected the messages and dated drafts and raised it calmly, then began sending written updates so everyone saw who did what. Amandeep first felt bitter after the promotion, then started a Friday summary that made the work visible.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling in the Monday meeting?
qa.a: She felt angry and used. Her face went hot and her jaw tightened.

qa.q: What could Avni do if it happened again?
qa.a: She could take the dated messages and drafts to the manager as plain facts.

grounding: One colleague presents another's work as their own, which brings anger and betrayal to the one wronged and bitterness to a bystander who then learns to make work visible.
